title: Nepal-China border floods death toll climbs to 1,385 as thousands remain missing - TRT World
description: Nepal-China border floods death toll climbs to 1,385 as thousands remain missing  TRT World
publisher.title: TRT World
full_article:
The death toll from devastating flash floods in Nepal has reached at least 1,342, with thousands still missing, officials and local media reports have said.

The combined death toll from flash floods and mudslides along the Nepal-China border rose to at least 1,385, while 5,519 people remained missing 11 days after the disaster struck, according to official data from the two countries on Sunday.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said around 5,000 people, including 589 foreigners, remained missing.

More than 13,000 people have so far been rescued from the flood-hit areas.

Chinese authorities said at least 43 people have been confirmed dead, while 519 others remained missing in Tibet.

Of those missing, 850 are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.

Related TRT World - Rescuers pull Chinese national alive from Nepal tunnel after 10 days

‘We are not getting enough to eat’

With roads and bridges damaged due to massive floods and landslides, thousands of expectant and new mothers are struggling hardest to find a female-friendly space to breastfeed, get proper food and reach emergency care if labour turns dangerous, the local English daily Kathmandu Post reported.

The mothers also complain about cigarette smoke, the smell of alcohol and, on top of all that, unhygienic food and water, which upset their and their babies' stomachs.

Also, there are no vaccination facilities for children in the shelter camps.

"We are not getting food on time either. We are not getting enough to eat,” a new mother who wished to be identified only as Pariyar said.

Pariyar fled her home when floods struck her hometown, Trishuli, on the morning of August 26 and is now staying with dozens of strangers under one roof in a shelter camp.

full_article:
The United Nations’ top official in Nepal has issued an emotional appeal for international aid, warning that survivors of the catastrophic Himalayan flooding last month saw their lives transformed “in one to two minutes”.

The UN Resident Coordinator, Lila Pieters Yahia, said communities along the China-Nepal border were struggling to comprehend the scale of devastation after torrential floods on August 26 tore through mountain districts, destroying roads, bridges and hydropower dams.

“You lose your home, you lose your livelihood, you lose your loved one and you lose the breadwinner of your family,” she told the AFP news agency in Kathmandu. “And you know, this happened in one to two minutes.”

At least 1,384 people were killed and more than 5,500 others remain missing in Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Among the missing are more than 800 foreigners from at least 34 countries, including tourists and pilgrims.

Many communities near the epicentre remain cut off, with roads washed away and journeys that once took hours now stretching into days. The UN, working with Nepal’s government, has launched a $50m appeal to support more than 84,000 people affected.

The UN’s Pieters Yahia warned of the risk of cholera and other communicable diseases, citing the deaths of 5,000 cattle and urging urgent investment in sanitation, hygiene and protection for vulnerable women and girls.

“My plea to the international community is: this is the time to help Nepal,” she said. “We can’t leave them alone.”

title: Middle Tennessee woman among spiritual travelers who died in Nepal flood - Chattanooga Times Free Press
description: Middle Tennessee woman among spiritual travelers who died in Nepal flood  Chattanooga Times Free Press
publisher.title: Chattanooga Times Free Press
full_article:
As soon as Leslie Crespi heard the news about the floods in Nepal, she put on her shoes and ran out her door to make her way to a friend’s house. On Aug. 26, flash flooding on the Nepal-China border led to buildings and towns being washed away, and the combined death toll has surpassed 950 people as of Monday, according to the Associated Press. At the time the flood hit, a group of 80 people from the Isha Foundation — 77 travelers and three volunteers who were helping guide the group — were at a Chinese immigration center at the Nepal-China border, returning from their two-week trip. Officials told the Isha Foundation that there is no indication of survivors in the area, Crespi said. Out of the 77 travelers, 22 were American, 12 were Canadian and the rest of the group was made up of people from 19 other countries, Crespi said. Crespi serves as the community liaison for the Isha Institute of Inner-Sciences, a center dedicated to classical yoga and meditation practices with the goal of raising human consciousness, she said. The center, based in McMinnville, Tennessee, is part of the international Isha Foundation, which had groups of people traveling in the Himalayas on what the organization calls a sojourn to Lake Manasarovar and Mount Kailash in Tibet. The foundation is not releasing the identities of those who were lost in the floods out of respect for their families. Many of the Americans and Canadians who were at the flooded immigration center had come through the center in McMinnville, Crespi said, so the news brings personal grief. “Initially, when we first heard the information, everybody goes into shock,” Crespi said. “This was so unexpected and the hit on that building was so devastating that it’s hard to take in, but we had to support the families immediately.” One of the 22 Americans on the sojourn was a wife and mother from Middle Tennessee, Crespi said, and the woman’s husband and family were Crespi’s first visit. Crespi, alongside other volunteers, has been gathering information from authorities in China and Nepal and distributing it to families in the days following the catastrophe. “Just a lot of silent support,” Crespi said. “Honestly, we were trying to do whatever was needed in each situation.” The Isha Foundation was established 30 years ago, Crespi said, by Sadhguru (born Jagadish Vasudev), an Indian spiritual guru. There are five main centers, two in the United States — in Los Angeles, California, and McMinnville, Tennessee. The Institute of Inner-Sciences in McMinnville was established in 2005, Crespi said. The foundation has been doing this type of trip for 21 years, she said. The people on the trip came from all walks of life — all kinds of religions, traditions, nationalities and ages. Crespi herself has been to Kailash twice. “Being on that soil, walking on that soil, looking at the faces of those people, those gentle, beautiful people that are there … these are the people that are from the region that support you along the journey,” Crespi said. “It’s heartbreaking because, you know, this is a hugely spiritual part of the world, and to see to see the level of devastation right now, it’s humongous.” There were more than 700 additional travelers with the Isha Foundation and Sadhguru still on the Tibet side when the floods hit, Crespi said. Those people were all safe, and are on their way back to their homes. Since the flooding, Sadhguru hosted an event in Kathmandu called “In Solidarity with Nepal,” calling for nations around the world to support the region, Crespi said. The plan was for this year to be Sadhguru’s last sojourn, but now, he plans to return, Crespi said. “Looking at the scale of destruction, it looks bad,” Sadhguru said in a video message recorded on Aug. 26 and posted to the Isha Foundation’s website. “The same building where we were for immigration just a week ago, that entire building is washed away, and part of the town is washed away.” The guru had tears in his eyes as he choked through the information he had on the group, and the audience behind the camera can be heard weeping. Sadhguru said in the video that he had passed by the group while they were on their way down Mount Kailash and he and his group were on their way up. Sadhguru recieved a message from the group’s guide at 9:05 a.m. that they had arrived at the immigration center, and the floods swept through at 9:14 a.m., he said in the video. The guide had a Nepali phone that would have become active if the group had crossed over into the country, but the phone never came online, Sadhguru said. The first day or two were dedicated to relaying information to families, but now, the reality is sinking in. Crespi is leaning on the yoga and meditation techniques she learned when she first came to the Isha Foundation over 20 years ago, she said, to handle the grief. “Right now for me, I’m recognizing the painful reality of the situation,” Crespi said. “At 42, I learned to meditate, and I have to tell you, it’s been an anchoring thing for me throughout this. It keeps me at a certain level of centeredness and clarity and perception. It doesn’t mean there’s no pain. There’s definitely a deep pain and compassion, but there’s a certain stability that moves you forward, and that has been a godsend.” Contact faith and family editor Kailee Shores at kshores@timesfreepress.com or 423-757-6659.

title: Chinese worker rescued after 10 days trapped in Nepal tunnel - KHGI
description: Chinese worker rescued after 10 days trapped in Nepal tunnel  KHGI
publisher.title: KHGI
full_article:
(TNND) — Ten days after catastrophic flash floods tore through Nepal’s mountains, rescuers pulled a Chinese worker from a mud-filled hydropower tunnel, a rare moment of relief amid a disaster that has killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands unaccounted for.

The flash floods struck Nepal and China’s Tibet region on Aug. 26, likely after a glacier collapse. Nepal’s disaster management agency said nearly 4,900 people remain missing. Earlier in the response, authorities reported more than 3,700 people had been rescued in Nepal.

On the Tibet side of the border, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported 43 deaths and 519 people missing as of Saturday evening. CCTV said 261 of those missing were foreigners.

Rescue operations have focused in part on hydropower sites in Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the devastated Gyirong border crossing in Tibet. Authorities previously believed more than 100 people could be trapped inside a mud-filled tunnel at the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project.

CCTV reported that Lu Haitao, a 49-year-old Chinese worker, was rescued Saturday from a 225-meter, or roughly 740-foot, hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa, 10 days after the floods. Rescuers carried Lu out of the tunnel and evacuated him by helicopter, according to CCTV, which reported he was hospitalized in stable condition.

Lu told CCTV he had climbed to the highest point in the tunnel and had begun to lose hope before rescue crews found him. CCTV reported Lu is a former farmer from Henan province who also worked as a carpenter, and that he traveled to Nepal in February for his first job abroad.

As the search continues, families of missing people have searched hospitals and relief centers and posted photographs and contact information in hopes of finding relatives.

Rescue work has been complicated by steep mountains, narrow gorges and concern about further flooding from a lake that formed in the Himalayas after the initial disaster. Chinese monitoring data showed the water level in that new lake had dropped about 10 meters, or 32 feet, from its peak.

Nepal said it mobilized domestic and international resources, including an 11-member tunnel-rescue reconnaissance team from India. A similar team from China was expected.

Nepal has received more than 57 metric tons of relief supplies from India, with aid also arriving from China, Japan, Australia and other countries.

(टीएनएनडी) : नेपाल केरऽ पहाड़ऽ क॑ फाड़ला के दस दिन बाद बचावकर्मी न॑ चीनी मजदूर क॑ कीचड़ स॑ भरलऽ जलविद्युत सुरंग स॑ खींच॑ लेलकै, जे एगो ऐसनऽ आपदा के बीच राहत केरऽ दुर्लभ क्षण छेकै जेकरा म॑ १३०० स॑ भी अधिक लोगऽ के मौत होय गेलऽ छै आरू हजारों लोगऽ के हिसाब-किताब नै होय गेलऽ छै ।

नेपाल आरू चीन केरऽ तिब्बत क्षेत्र म॑ २६ अगस्त क॑ आकस्मिक बाढ़ आबी गेलऽ छेलै, जेकरऽ संभावना ग्लेशियर केरऽ गिरला के बाद होय गेलऽ छै । नेपाल के आपदा प्रबंधन एजेंसी के कहनाय छनि जे करीब 4900 लोक लापता अछि. एहि सं पहिने प्रतिक्रिया मे अधिकारी नेपाल मे 3700 सं बेसि लोक के बचाओल गेल अछि.

सीमा के तिब्बत तरफ चीनी सरकारी प्रसारक सीसीटीवी में शनिदिन साँझ तक 43 लोक के मौत आ 519 लोक के लापता होय के खबर अछि. सीसीटीवी के कहनाय अछि जे लापता मे सं 261 गोटे विदेशी छथिन्ह.

बचाव कार्य कुछ हद तक नेपाल केरऽ रसुवा जिला केरऽ जलविद्युत स्थल आरू तिब्बत केरऽ तबाह ग्यरोंग सीमा पार प॑ केंद्रित छै । अधिकारि सब के पहिने विश्वास छल जे अपर त्रिशुली-1 जलविद्युत परियोजना के कीचड़ सं भरल सुरंग के अंदर 100 सं बेसी लोक फंसल भ सकैत अछि.

सीसीटीवी के खबर छै कि बाढ़ के 10 दिन बाद शनिदिन रसुवा के 225 मीटर यानी लगभग 740 फीट के जलविद्युत सुरंग स॑ 49 वर्षीय चीनी मजदूर लु हैताओ क॑ बचाय लेलऽ गेलै । सीसीटीवी के अनुसार बचावकर्मी लु क॑ सुरंग स॑ बाहर निकाली क॑ हेलीकॉप्टर स॑ बाहर निकाली लेलकै, जेकरा म॑ हुनकऽ हालत स्थिर अस्पताल म॑ भर्ती होय के खबर छै ।

title: Nepal Flood Disaster - Caritas Australia
description: Nepal Flood Disaster  Caritas Australia
publisher.title: Caritas Australia
full_article:
The full scale of the disaster is continuing to emerge. Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands are missing. Entire communities have been destroyed, roads and bridges have been washed away, and thousands of families have been displaced.

The disaster was triggered by a massive flood surge through the Bhote Koshi River on 26 August, devastating communities across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other downstream districts. Rescue operations remain underway, but damaged infrastructure and ongoing flood risks continue to limit access to many affected communities.

The humanitarian needs remain immense. Families urgently require food, clean water, shelter, health care and essential household items. Schools and health facilities have also been damaged, and humanitarian assessments indicate that thousands of children need support.

WEST HARTFORD, Conn. (WFSB) - Connecticut’s Nepali community gathered Sunday evening at West Hartford Town Hall for a candlelight vigil honoring those killed and missing after flash floods in Nepal’s Bhote Koshi Valley.

Dozens attended the vigil, and organizers said the gathering was meant to remember those who lost their lives and to support families still waiting for answers.

Families await word from Nepal

Many families in Connecticut’s Nepali community have relatives and friends in the areas hit by the floods, and some are still waiting to hear from loved ones.

As of Sept. 3, Nepal’s disaster authority reported about 1,252 people dead and more than 4,200 people still missing.

Vigil draws young and old

Those gathered said they are holding on to hope and doing what they can to support those affected back home.

Bishesh Pariyar, 8, said, “I just feel sad, worried about all my family stuck in Nepal with the flood.”

Kashbi Kandel, 14, said, “We’re sending prayers for them, hoping their okay and everything will be okay and we will move past this.”

title: Bangladesh sought more energy from Nepal, but floods have halted exports - Eco-Business
description: Bangladesh sought more energy from Nepal, but floods have halted exports  Eco-Business
publisher.title: Eco-Business
full_article:
Monsoon rains have routinely given Nepal a surge of hydropower, creating a surplus. Some of that surplus was used to supplement downstream neighbour Bangladesh’s fossil-fuel-dependent electricity supply.

On 26 August, however, Nepal’s hydropower system was damaged extensively. Flash floods swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems, killing at least 1,250 people as of 3 September. The floods also damaged 15 hydropower plants and critical transmission infrastructure, wiping out over 750 MW of electricity generation, reported Time. Nearly 900 hydropower workers are missing.

The disaster has now disrupted Nepal’s electricity exports, with supplies to Bangladesh halted, authorities in Dhaka and Kathmandu confirmed to Dialogue Earth.

On 3 September, Shaligram Bhandari, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, told Dialogue Earth that floods damaged the 22 megawatt (MW) Chilime and 24 MW Trishuli hydropower projects, which have since stopped generating electricity. The power they produced had been approved for export to Bangladesh. Nepal halted all power exports, Reuters reported several days earlier.

Amid the disaster, the ministry had yet to explore alternatives, Bhandari said.

Nepal’s growing role as a hydropower exporter must be viewed together with these vulnerabilities.

“ Hydropower from Nepal and Bhutan could provide Bangladesh with a cheaper source of electricity than many of the country’s existing generation sources. Shafiqul Alam, lead analyst for Bangladesh, Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis

Complicating its role as an exporter is its lack of a shared border with Bangladesh. Electricity trade between them has passed through India’s transmission network, which comes with some conditions.

Since 2024, Nepal has been exporting 40 MW of electricity to Bangladesh through India’s network every June to November. It wanted to export 20 MW more. But this June, the Indian power trading company which manages cross-border grid operations with Bangladesh declined the request, Nepali government officials told the Kathmandu Post. The company, NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam Limited, reportedly cited capacity constraints on the India-Bangladesh transmission line.

In July, India held energy cooperation talks with Nepal. While there was development on bilateral energy coordination, there was no resolution on the 20 MW issue.

That amount is minuscule compared to the size of the three countries’ electricity grids, which have a combined total installed capacity of around 586 GW. But energy experts, officials and power-sector analysts in those countries told Dialogue Earth the 20 MW impasse is more nuanced than it appears. There are technical, procedural and political factors at play, they note.

The disruption in Nepal comes at a particularly difficult time for Bangladesh, which has experienced severe load-shedding in recent days. It faced a power shortfall exceeding 3,500 MW at one point, as well as widespread outages across the country. The loss of electricity from Nepal only adds to that pressure.

While Bangladeshi and Nepali experts point to unused capacity on the India-Bangladesh transmission link, Indian experts say there could be a genuine capacity limitation on the line. In the absence of a regional body and trade mechanism dedicated to energy, procedural lapses and politics also have major roles to play, they note. Strained India-Bangladesh relations since Bangladesh’s 2024 change of government may also be involved.

Why Bangladesh wants Nepal’s hydropower

Nepal and Bangladesh have complementary electricity needs. The summer monsoon gives Nepal surplus hydropower, which Bangladesh can use to diversify its energy sources. In the dry winter, these roles reverse somewhat – Nepal faces shortages while Bangladesh’s demand dips – making cross-border trade beneficial in both directions over the year.

In 2025-2026, Nepal’s total installed capacity reached 4.1 GW, but monthly peak domestic demand stood at only around 2.5 GW, according to the Nepal Energy Authority. Electricity exports bring total demand up to about 3.2 GW.

Bangladesh has 32 GW of installed power generation capacity, 98 per cent of which is dependent on fossil fuels, according to energy think-tank Ember. The country wants to diversify sources to meet its current demand. Bangladesh also aims to cover 20 per cent of its electricity needs from non-imported renewables by 2030. Energy trade between Nepal and Bangladesh therefore makes “economic sense”, says Shahriar Ahmed Chowdhury, director of the Centre for Energy Research at United International University in Dhaka. “Hydropower from Nepal and Bhutan could provide Bangladesh with a cheaper source of electricity than many of the country’s existing generation sources,” says Shafiqul Alam, lead analyst for Bangladesh energy at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. “Ideally, electricity trade should work both ways,” Chowdhury says. But expanding such trade is “a political decision”, he notes. “The volume is small, but it is important because it marks the beginning of cross-border electricity cooperation.” Cross-border electricity trade helps Bangladesh primarily by shielding it from geopolitical disruptions to energy supplies, volatility in international fuel prices and diversification, experts say. After all, the additional 20 MW will not help Bangladesh meet its 20 per cent renewables target. There is no plan to include imports within what is a domestic generation target, says Aninda Islam Amit, Bangladesh’s state minister for power, energy and mineral resources. He expects the country’s private sector to “take the lead” on renewables as there are “incentives for private entrepreneurs”, he tells Dialogue Earth. For Nepal, the energy trade is part of a much larger ambition. During the July energy talks, it agreed to increase its export capacity as India ups its import capacity. Nepali energy minister Birajbhakta Shrestha tells Dialogue Earth that the deal is another step towards fulfilling the country’s agreement to export 10 GW of electricity to India, signed in 2024. A Nepali energy ministry official, requesting anonymity, says the immediate 20-MW issue could be resolved through trilateral discussions between Nepal, India and Bangladesh. India holds the missing link The 40 MW Nepal currently exports to Bangladesh is transported by the Baharampur-Bheramara high-voltage DC interconnection from east India, where it arrives on a transmission line from southern Nepal. The Baharampur-Bheramara link between India and Bangladesh has a transfer capacity of 1 GW. The country typically receives around 920-930 MW through the link, leaving some unused transfer capacity, said a Bangladesh Power Division official speaking on condition of anonymity. Nepal has also been considering alternatives. “If power cannot be exported via the Baharampur-Bheramara line, there is option for Nepal to export the additional 20 MW through other Indian transmission lines connected to Bangladesh,” says Manoj Silwal, former deputy managing director of the Nepal Electricity Authority. Apart from the Baharampur-Bheramara link, Bangladesh also imports nearly 1.7 GW from India: 160 MW through the Surajmaninagar to Comilla interconnection, and 1.5 GW from Godda to Rohanpur, the latter operated by Adani Power. However, transporting the 20 MW via existing corridors may not be feasible for a few reasons, says Nikit Abhyankar, an energy efficiency expert at the University of California, Berkeley. It is possible that these corridors are fully utilised. Additionally, the average amount of electricity a transmission line carries is not necessarily the capacity that is safely available, Abhyankar notes. At times of peak demand, power flows can be much higher, and some capacity must be reserved to manage unexpected failures elsewhere in the system. “I would be very surprised if they are actually going to operate a 1,000 MW line at 1,000 MW capacity,” Abhyankar says. A line may also be unable to deliver its rated amount of electricity due to losses from transfers. In a high-voltage DC connection, such as Baharampur-Bheramara, some electricity is lost when power is converted from AC to DC, as it travels along the transmission line, and when converted back to AC at the receiving end. Abhyankar estimates that roughly 40-50 MW could be lost on a 1-GW line. The Baharampur-Bheramara corridor is also loaded with India’s own exports to Bangladesh. India’s Central Electricity Authority “doesn’t want to run the line close to its thermal limit … on a line that also carries India’s own bilateral exports”, notes Binit Das, deputy programme manager for renewable energy at the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE). For the India-Bangladesh link, battery storage could potentially help if the line has spare capacity during periods of lower demand, Abhyankar adds. But feasibility depends on how much the power flow on the interconnection varies over the day. Politics complicates power trade Geography presents India with an unavoidable role in any future Nepal-Bangladesh electricity trade. “There is no other way that Bangladesh can get power from either Nepal or Bhutan without that being facilitated by India,” says Bipul Chattopadhyay, executive director of the Consumer Unity & Trust Society (CUTS), India. Experts see this 20 MW episode as a litmus test for how India prioritises capacity across competing uses of a shared asset. During this impasse, India and Nepal separately reached a much bigger capacity decision: to raise Nepal’s export quota from 1.1 GW to 1.65 GW. “The asymmetry between how quickly that bilateral decision happened and how long the trilateral 20 MW has languished is itself the clearest evidence of where the region’s integration problem actually sits,” says Das of the CSE. India’s role in Nepal’s hydropower sector also complicates the picture. Several Indian companies are developing major hydropower projects in Nepal, while India is also Nepal’s principal electricity export market and the transit country for its exports to Bangladesh. India could increasingly draw on Nepal’s hydropower to meet its own rising demand, Chattopadhyay says. The challenge is to develop a framework that works for all the countries involved. “It should be win-win for all three parties,” he says. “That model is not difficult to develop, but that is something which is still missing in our current political-economic discourse.” He also raises political considerations in the 20-MW denial. Relations between India and Bangladesh have been strained since former prime minister of Bangladesh, Sheikh Hasina, went into exile in India in August 2024, where she remains. “After the change in government in Bangladesh, [the] India-Bangladesh relationship is yet to get on the right track … it’s very frosty,” notes Chattopadhyay. A South Asian electricity market? The difficulty of moving a mere 20 MW points to bottlenecks in cross-border energy trade in a region with growing energy needs. Every prior expansion of the transmission corridor, including the original 40 MW, was formalised through a Joint Steering Committee (JSC) decision followed by a tripartite agreement. The 13th Nepal-India JSC meeting was held in July, having last convened in February 2025, but failed to yield success with the 20 MW addition. There is also a broader institutional problem. Cross-border electricity trade between Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal, where it goes through India, requires multiple layers of approval. This includes a tripartite power sale agreement, clearance from India’s Central Electricity Authority and a JSC to anchor the decision. Over the last few years, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal have signed bilateral agreements with India to develop electricity trade. As of April, India has entered into 17 power-sector agreements with neighbouring countries. It is also involved in 13 cross-border power-generation projects and 30 transmission-link projects. Trilateral and regional transactions carry a layer of political and procedural friction that bilateral ones don’t, Das says. This makes the region’s power systems interconnected yet fragmented. The potential benefits of deeper integration are significant. Cross-border electricity trade can allow these countries to complement one another’s demands, reducing reliance on fossil fuels while improving energy security and lowering costs, joint research by CUTS and Chintan Research Foundation found. The stakes are also different for countries of different sizes. “For a large system like India … small cross-border trade doesn’t really make a huge difference. But for countries like Nepal to sell their hydroelectricity [and] for countries like Bangladesh to meet their electricity demand reliably, cross-border trade becomes important,” says Abhyankar. Yet there is still no subregional institution focused on coordinating and facilitating cross-border electricity trade. A regional power exchange, an agreed open-access framework, or institutionalised, calendar-bound trilateral bodies could provide a more predictable way of handling third-country transit, says Das. “Without such a mechanism, episodes like the 20-MW holdup could continue to recur even as the region’s growing hydropower surplus and complementary electricity demand make the case for trade increasingly obvious,” he says. न॑ नोट करलकै । पीक डिमांड कें समय बिजली कें प्रवाह बहुत बेसि भ सकय छै, आ सिस्टम मे अन्य जगहक पर अप्रत्याशित विफलता कें प्रबंधन कें लेल किच्छू क्षमता आरक्षित करनाय आवश्यक छै. अभिनकर कहैत छथि जे अगर ओ वास्तव मे 1000 मेगावाट क क्षमता पर 1000 मेगावाट क लाइन चलाबए जा रहल छथि त हमरा बहुत आश्चर्य होएत। कोनों लाइन ट्रांसफर सं नुकसान कें कारण अपन रेटेड राशि कें बिजली सेहो नहि पहुंचा सकय छै. हाई-वोल्टेज डीसी कनेक्शन, जेना कि बहारमपुर-भेरामरा मे, जखन बिजली कें एसी सं डीसी मे बदलल जायत छै, कियाकि इ ट्रांसमिशन लाइन कें साथ चलै छै, आ जखन रिसीविंग एंड पर वापस एसी मे बदलल जायत छै, तखन किछ बिजली कें नुकसान बिजली प्राधिकरण “अपनऽ तापीय सीमा के करीब लाइन क॑ नै चलाबै चाहै छै ... ऐन्हऽ लाइन प॑ जे भारत केरऽ अपनऽ द्विपक्षीय निर्यात भी ले जाय छै”, सेंटर फॉर साइंस एंड एनवायरनमेंट (सीएसई) केरऽ अक्षय ऊर्जा केरऽ डिप्टी प्रोग्राम मैनेजर बिनित दास न॑ नोट करलकै । अभिनकर आरू कहै छै कि भारत-बांग्लादेश लिंक लेली बैटरी स्टोरेज संभावित रूप स॑ मदद करी सकै छै अगर कम मांग के दौरान लाइन म॑ स्पेयर क्षमता छै । मुदा विद्युत व्यापार में अपरिहार्य भूमिका के सामने पेश करै छै । भारत केरऽ कंज्यूमर यूनिटी एंड ट्रस्ट सोसाइटी (सीयूटीएस) केरऽ कार्यकारी निदेशक बिपुल चट्टोपाध्याय न॑ कहलकै कि भारत केरऽ सहायता के बिना न॑ कहलकै कि वू द्विपक्षीय फैसला कतनी जल्दी होय गेलै आरू त्रिपक्षीय २० मेगावाट कतनी देर स॑ सुस्त रहलऽ छै, ई बात के बीच के विषमता ही ई सबस॑ स्पष्ट सबूत छै कि ई क्षेत्र केरऽ एकीकरण के समस्या वास्तव म॑ अछि। पिछला किछु साल स बांग्लादेश, भूटान आ नेपाल भारत क संग बिजली व्यापार क विकास लेल द्विपक्षीय समझौता पर हस्ताक्षर केलक अछि। अप्रैल तक भारत पड़ोसी देशक संग 17 बिजली क्षेत्रक समझौता कएने अछि। इ सीमा आकार के देश के लेल सेहो दांव अलग-अलग अछि. अभिनकर कहै छै, "भारत जैसनऽ बड़ऽ सिस्टम लेली ... सीमा पार स॑ छोटऽ व्यापार स॑ वास्तव म॑ बहुत बड़ऽ फर्क नै पड़ै छै ।लेकिन नेपाल जैसनऽ देश लेली अपनऽ जलविद्युत full_article:
Video footage showing the tense moment when the Korea Disaster Relief Team (KDRT) rescued a Chinese survivor of the Nepal flash flood was released by Korean authorities on Sunday.

“Are you okay?” a Korean rescuer asked as they pointed the flashlight toward what appeared to be a human figure.

As Korean rescuers approached closer, they confirmed the survivor was waiting on a platform above the flood debris inside the tunnel.

Related Article Far from home, Nepali students in Korea grapple with tragedy of flood

With the rescuers' instructions and assistance, the survivor climbed down from the platform on his own using an attached metal beam.

The survivor was wearing a full-sleeve T-shirt and only boxer shorts. He was not wearing shoes.

“When the rescuers’ light shone on me, I could not shout back because I could not believe that they were here to save me,” the survivor told Chinese broadcaster CCTV.

A Chinese survivor trapped inside a tunnel smiles as Korean rescuers come to save him in footage carried by Yonhap News TV. KOREA DISASTER RELIEF TEAM

The footage was recorded with a camera attached to the Korean rescuers' helmets. The clip also showed the rescuers wading through mud that reached their upper torsos.

The Chinese survivor was found inside a 225-meter-long (738-foot-long) tunnel and was later transported to a military hospital by helicopter.

The survivor was found at the hydropower plant construction site where the nine missing Koreans had been working. One Korean is believed to be near the weir dam, close to where the survivor was found, while the other eight are believed to be farther downstream.

The KDRT plans to continue the search mission inside the tunnel, as the survivor said another person was nearby, though he did not know whether the person was alive.

Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun is also set to hold ministerial talks with his Nepali counterpart regarding rescue efforts to find missing Koreans.





BY LEE SOO-JUNG [lee.soojung1@joongang.co.kr]

title: Nepal Condolence motion - Australian Minister for Foreign Affairs
description: Nepal Condolence motion  Australian Minister for Foreign Affairs
publisher.title: Australian Minister for Foreign Affairs
full_article:
President, the devastation we have witnessed in Nepal and Tibet, China has been catastrophic.

We have seen the terrifying force of floodwaters tear through towns and villages — homes, roads and bridges swept away. The scale of the destruction, almost beyond comprehension.

Families have lost loved ones. Thousands – thousands — of people remain missing.

And amongst them are 36 Australians.

I want to acknowledge how distressing this time is for their loved ones – and how much harder this becomes with every day that passes.

Every hour without news is another hour of waiting, of hoping and of fearing.

The Australian Government is doing all we can to find Australians who remain unaccounted for, to support loved ones and to assist in the disaster response.

We have deployed almost 50 officers to the region to support search, rescue, and recovery efforts.

Officials in Kathmandu, Beijing, New Delhi and Canberra are working around the clock to establish the whereabouts of Australians, meeting directly with family members who have travelled to Nepal, desperate for information, seeking answers from local authorities, tour operators, from hospitals, and other organisations – pursuing every possible avenue for information.

Dedicated case officers from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Australian Federal Police have been assigned to support the next of kin of those missing – giving families a consistent point of contact in an unimaginably difficult time.

In addition to this, two Services Australia social workers arrived in Kathmandu last night and a dedicated family support hub is being set up by our Embassy.

From the outset, the Australian Government has made clear that we stood ready to help Nepal, including on search and rescue efforts.

And we continue to offer assistance to China.

Specialist Australian drone operators have now travelled to Nepal as part of a 15-person Disaster Assistance Response Team.

Drawn from Fire and Rescue New South Wales and the Queensland Fire Department, they bring advanced technology capable of rapid mapping, imaging, and supporting searches in extraordinarily challenging terrain.

AFP Disaster Victim Identification specialists are also deploying to Nepal.

And we have provided telecommunication data to Nepali authorities with the hope that this may narrow the last known location of missing Australians.

We know most of the unaccounted-for Australians were last known to be in the Gyirong and Syabrubesi areas.

Nepali search and rescue teams are on the ground in both areas, and we are working directly with the authorities to gather any information we can.

Australia has committed $11 million in humanitarian assistance, supporting emergency shelter, food, clean water, sanitation, healthcare, and other essential supplies.

A Royal Australian Air Force C-17 has delivered almost 24 tonnes of humanitarian aid to Nepal.

And Australians themselves have responded with characteristic generosity, donating $4.5 million of their own money to the Emergency Action Alliance.

And we have matched the donations from the Australian people with a $5 million contribution from the Government to the EAA.

Colleagues, we know the grief and anxiety of this disaster reached deeply into our communities.

Australia’s Nepali community is grieving for family, friends, and communities in the region.

Members of Australia’s Tibetan community are too experiencing great anguish.

And for many Hindu Australians, including those with connections to the pilgrimage routes and sacred places of this region, this disaster has brought deep sorrow.

To each of these communities, we extend the sympathy and solidary of this Parliament.

The search, rescue and recovery response continues. And we know the road ahead will be long.

Infrastructure must be rebuilt. Communities will need shelter and essential services will need to be restored.

Families will need support long after the immediate phase of this emergency response has passed.

We will continue to stand with Nepal through that long road of recovery.

Ready to provide further search, rescue and recovery assistance where needed.

Today, this Senate mourns all those who have lost their lives. And we hold close those still waiting for news.

We thank the responders, in Nepal, in Tibet, China, and from Australia, who continue their work in very difficult circumstances.

And on behalf of the Australian Government, I extend my deepest condolences to all those affected.

title: Nepali community rallies for flood victims in West Hartford - NBC Connecticut
description: Nepali community rallies for flood victims in West Hartford  NBC Connecticut

full_article:
The Nepali community gathered Sunday in West Hartford to mourn the victims of devastating floods in Nepal and raise money for relief efforts more than a week after the disaster.

More than 1,300 people have died and more than 5,000 remain missing across Nepal and China after flooding that was likely triggered by a glacier collapse.

Stream Connecticut News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. WATCH HERE

In West Hartford, community members lit candles and arranged them around the flag of Nepal during a vigil for those affected by the disaster.

“We’re sending prayers and hoping they’re okay,” 14-year-old Kashvi Kandeo of West Hartford said.

The flooding swept away buildings and people, leaving members of Connecticut’s Nepali community struggling to comprehend videos showing the destruction.

“It really hurts to see your home country get destroyed like this,” Kandeo said.

That shock has also prompted the community to take action. The vigil brought together members of the Nepali community as well as local and state leaders while raising money for relief efforts.

“Whenever these things happen, the whole community comes together and want to gather and try to support it,” West Hartford resident Pramod Pradhan said.

West Hartford is home to one of Connecticut’s largest Nepali communities, with about 1,000 Nepali people living in Hartford County, based on data compiled by the Asian and Asian American Studies Institute at UConn.

Vigil organizers said they have collectively raised a few thousand dollars to support relief efforts.

Community members said the disaster has also demonstrated the resilience of the Nepali people.

“They’re really strong for that because so much has happened and the fact that they can keep pushing forward it just really shows how strong they are,” Kandeo said.

Organizers in West Hartford are asking people who want to contribute to relief efforts in Nepal to donate directly to the Nepalese government. That can be found here.

title: A local woman is finding ways to help family and community back in Nepal - kimt.com
description: A local woman is finding ways to help family and community back in Nepal  kimt.com
publisher.title: kimt.com
full_article:
MINNEAPOLIS (WCCO) -- For Jeena Gurung Vomhof, the Minnesota State Fair was supposed to be a celebration.

A chance to share the art and traditions of the country she still calls home.

Then came devastating news from Nepal.

"I was almost done with the set up to be selling at the 2026 Minnesota State Fair. Excited, pumped, you know, new space, new energy, and I couldn't, I couldn't see my social media, like what's happening. It was like, that was not real to me. And I just called my mom and said what's happening," said Gurung Vomhof.

Gurung Vomhof is originally from Kathmandu.

Nepal is home to Gurung Vomhof's family, her memories, and the women whose work she brings to Minnesota.

"Nepal is a beautiful country. It's an Asian country, right below China and above India, surrounded by beautiful mountains, beautiful people, the tradition, the culture, the love, the humanity that is there in the country I still miss and I try to bring that wherever I go," explained Gurung Vomhof.

Through her business, Namaste Brows & Boutique in Roseville, Gurung Vomhof employs sixteen women in Nepalmaking — hand-crafted earrings, cashmere shawls, hemp, and felt gift items. 100% of the proceeds go back to the makers.

"Each and every piece that I sell has a story," said Gurung Vomhof.

But right now, she's carrying a story of loss.

"My friends, my family, who are far and close, are still back home and we have lost two cousins, 21 and 35, who were going trekking. They're missing," said Gurung Vomhof.

She talks with family every day, trying to stay connected while holding herself together.

At the fair, people she doesn't know are giving her something she needs right now.

"My favorite thing right now is hugs. You know, when I'm holding all of this, I don't know how, I have the right word physically, emotionally. Joy, hurt? That hug means so much," said Gurung Vomhof

Those moments are helping her keep going.

She's already thinking beyond the immediate crisis - about children, education, and rebuilding.

"Education is the root of everything, everything. For me, maybe I can build a classroom, but I can't do it alone. I need all of you," said Gurung Vomhof.

For now, she'll keep standing for Nepal, sharing its culture, and believing in the people standing with her.

"I am at the grandstand at the lower level, row number nine, wide open with colors, with joy, and I'm going to be standing here every single minute," said Gurung Vomhof.

गुरुंग वोम्होफ कहलकै, "हम निचला स्तर के ग्रांडस्टैंड पर छियै, पंक्ति नंबर नौ, रंगऽ स॑ चौड़ा खुललऽ छियै, खुशी स॑, आरू हम्में हर एक मिनट म॑ एत॑ खड़ा रहबै ल॑ जाय रहलऽ छियै।"

एहि कथाक अपडेट लेल एतय क्लिक करू
